newsitem.title: GERMANY: Room where Berlin Wall's fall began goes to museum.
newsitem.headline: Room where Berlin Wall's fall began goes to museum.

text.p: The room where an East German Communist official announced the opening of the Berlin Wall is to be recreated and preserved in a museum, officials said on Tuesday.
The press briefing room was the scene of one of the most dramatic moments in postwar German history, on November 9, 1989.

Communist Party media chief Guenter Schabowski, towards the end of a routine news conference, read a statement saying East German citizens would be allowed to leave the country through border crossings.

His words spread like wildfire throughout the east and sent millions of East Germans pouring out onto the streets to see for themselves if they could really pass freely through the border for the first time since 1961.

Justice Minister Edzard Schmidt-Jortzig said in Berlin on Tuesday the briefing hall of the old East German International Press Centre could not be integrated into the united Germany's Justice Ministry, which is moving into the building.
The room's furniture and fittings will be moved to the Deutsche Museum in Berlin, where a replica based on its original dimensions is being recreated.

Many people in Berlin had asked that the briefing room be kept, but Schmidt-Jortzig said it would have cost 17 million marks ($11 million) to integrate the theatre-like hall with about 300 seats, into the ministry.
Schabowski's announcement made the Berlin Wall redundant and marked the effective end of the "Iron Curtain" along the border with West Germany.
The Wall had divided Berliners since the Communists erected fences and concrete barriers on August 13, 1961 to stem a westward flow of emigrants.
